Ive been job hopping since 2008 with a maximum duration of 4months at each job.
One or two jobs a year.

I know what to do but unsure how to present my case for an interview. Please I do not wish to lie or deter from the truth.
Best method to manage gaps in work history
You were working on independent projects! The project being finding a good job.
True it was beneficial to acquire some skills overall from all the jobs, the concern lies how the new job will feel about this because of the risk of leaving them too.

So do you have a long time since your last job? How'd you land those jobs if you've had 4 months per job, 2 jobs per year? Maybe you already know how to land a job if you've been job hopping since 2008! Think about what you've said to land all those jobs. Unless you've been fired you've obviously got a lot of experience in job interviews and have a somewhat diverse skill set. Making a bullet list of what you know and excel at might help with identifying what you are good at!
Excellent point. Although it has been a while since my last job (6months), enthusiasm played an important role at each interview.

Were you a contracted employee? Or were you salary? If you were contracted for specific jobs I see no problem. Just say you completed the tasks they hired you for and you moved on. If you were salary and you were fired or left for strange reasons you may want to flub the truth a little bit.

This is the answer, if you have been contracted for the work say so.

Else, the problem seems to be with you not being able to hold a position. For that, you should lie.
Mostly contracted employee and never salaried. What is flubbing the truth?
I think he means to give a diplomatic answer. like if you quit after yelling at your boss and walking out, instead say I left due to disagreements with management.

No...don't say that. Just let them know you completed the job you were hired to do. As someone who has hired others in the past, an applicant mentioning "disagreements with management" immediately lands you in the "nope" pile. Without knowing specifics, it just implies an inability to work out differences.
Fair point, but it's still better than saying you quit without notice.

If you do not want to lie or deter then you already know the answer. There is no sugar coating if you are job hopping for the sake of job hopping.

Are you getting bored at each job? Wanting a new experience? I am in a similar boat but I spend around 6 months to 2 years at each job. My last job was only 4 months because it was a terrible experience. I relayed that information to my interviewer and got the current job.
Great to hear you landed the current job! How are you doing there? After hopping different areas of IT, I've settled with networking.
I would suggest not applying for contract or contract to hire positions, and if they ask, be honest about looking for job stability, having done the constant shuffling already.

A whole series of short term jobs is a big red flag for me when I'm hiring for a permanent position. I hate hiring someone, spend all the time training them on our systems and such, and then have them leave after 6 months. I think of 1 year as the minimum amount of time that is "ok" to stay at an entry level job, and 2 years for a more senior position. I'll overlook one or two short-term stints if they have some long-term ones too, or if they are clearly contract positions, or if the candidate offers a clear explanation in their cover letter -- otherwise I routinely pass over otherwise qualified candidates because of this.

So for you, I'd say write a good cover letter (which, by the way, are sorely lacking in candidates these days!), and include something to the effect of "As you can see from my resume, I have experienced many varied positions with dynamic companies -- while this has been valuable and contributed to deepening my skills in X, Y, and Z, I am eager for the long-term stability of working at Foobar, Inc."

When interviewing, expect to be asked about the job hopping and why you left your various jobs -- especially the last couple, and any that resulted in extended periods of unemployment. It's hard to tell you precisely what to say during an interview without knowing your reasons for leaving your previous jobs, but never say anything directly negative about previous employers or supervisors.

I think the best advice I can give is to find someone (or two) to mock interview you -- ideally someone who actually interviews people IRL. Everyone has a different style and does things differently, but it's still really helpful experience.

Wow. Lay-duce is really laying on the "Kiryuu Nagisa is an insufferable prick" line heavy, and it's working. Thankfully, though, the bigger the asshole the more fulfilling the redemption (or cathartic the downfall).

One thing I've noticed, though, is that there's a bit of symbolic battle going on between Sera and Nagisa, insomuch as what they represent. Sera was described in episode one, jokingly, as "some sort of Showa-era Salaryman" when he described, in honest fervor, the joy of working in a corporate family. He's the very model of a 20th-century salaryman - sworn to the company, beholden to its values, and loyal to his coworkers. On the flip side of the coin we have the much more modernistic Nagisa, who embodies the profit-minded corporate style of modern businesses - I have no doubt the guy would burn down an orphanage if it meant profit.

The two business philosophies are staunchly at odds. The former creates less-profitable businesses with strong character and loyal employees; the latter creates highly-profitable, but soulless, corporations. This is made especially evident in Nagisa Kazuhisa's sass talk about the "sentimental notions" of the other founding family of the corporation. I'm looking forward to how the show will handle this sub-conflict; namely in how it'll tie into the (inevitable) conversion of Nagisa to Team A-TEC.
